newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia warning to protesters raises violence fears.
newsitem.headline: Serbia warning to protesters raises violence fears.

text.p: Serbian police have said opposition political rallies will no longer be permitted if they obstruct traffic, raising fears of violent confrontations.

"The police in Serbia will not tolerate the blockade of traffic in future and warn the organisers of the demonstrations that they must exercise their right to peaceful demonstrations in keeping with the regulations," said an Interior Ministry statement carried by the official Tanjug news agency late on Wednesday.
Observers said the statement's immediate effect on continued opposition demonstrations planned for the centre of Belgrade on Thursday was unclear.

Opponents of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic have blocked the centre of the capital for the past 36 days with massive protests triggered by the refusal of the ruling Socialists to acknowledge opposition victories in local elections.
The protests had been free of violence until Tuesday when surging crowds of pro and anti-Milosevic demonstrators clashed in the city.
Fifty-eight people were treated for injuries, including one man who was shot in the head and critically wounded.
West European states and the United States have warned Serbia that using force to obstruct demonstrations would jeopardise rump Yugoslavia's standing with the West.
Earlier on Wednesday, one of the leaders of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, Zoran Djindjic, said the authorities might be on the verge of banning future demonstrations.
He vowed at a news conference that the opposition would defy such a ban.

A split emerged between Russia and the West over policy towards Serbia on Wednesday as Moscow warned against outside interference in the Balkan republic while Washington, Paris and Bonn backed Belgrade's anti-government reformers.

Milosevic, widely viewed as the instigator of the Croatian and Bosnian wars, saw his reputation somewhat rehabilitated in 1995 when Europe and the United States relied on him to help broker and implement a Bosnian peace deal.
But Washington and Paris accused him of sparking Tuesday's violence by busing his supporters into Belgrade for a rally at the same time and place as an opposition demonstration.

More than a month of demonstrations went off peacefully before Milosevic and his Socialist party staged the counter-protest, an event which fell flat when only 40,000 supporters showed up compared to several hundred thousand opposition marchers.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said that any further violence would jeopardise Serbia's efforts to integrate with Europe.
Moscow took a different tack. Russia's Foreign Ministry issued a statement branding outside attempts to interfere in Serbian politics as "inadmissible".

The Russian comment was clearly aimed at Western efforts to pressure Milosevic into relaxing his grip on the media, police and judiciary -- a stranglehold which has given him dictatorial control over public life in Serbia.
Russia and the West were often at odds during the Bosnian war, sometimes working at cross-purposes in their efforts to contain and finally end the conflict.

Milosevic and his Bosnian Serb allies exploited the divisions, especially those between Moscow and Washington, to buy time and territory for Serb military forces and to shield them from NATO retaliation.

Milosevic is now apparently counting on Moscow to prevent the West from using the U.N. Security Council to reimpose economic sanctions which were lifted earlier this year in the wake of the Bosnian peace agreement.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is expected to present its findings on the deteriorating political situation in Serbia within the next week.
